lede: A two-year-old who cried on the Dragon Throne, lost his empire at six, was used by Japan as the puppet ruler of Manchuria, spent nine years in a Chinese prison, and ended his days as an ordinary clerk in Beijing.

ps: Aisin-Gioro Puyi was born in Beijing on 7 February 1906, into the Manchu imperial family that had ruled China since 1644 as the Qing dynasty. In 1908, aged two, he became emperor with the reign name Xuantong.

The revolution of 1911 ended the empire, and he abdicated in February 1912. He was allowed to keep his title and live in the inner Forbidden City, a boy emperor with no country, until he was thrown out in 1924.

Japan made him ruler of Manchukuo, a state it created in northeast China, from 1932 to 1945. After the war he was held by the Soviets, then imprisoned in the People's Republic of China, pardoned in 1959, and lived quietly in Beijing until his death in 1967.
His father was Zaifeng, Prince Chun, the brother of the Guangxu Emperor. The real power at court belonged to the old Empress Dowager Cixi.
In November 1908 the childless Guangxu Emperor died, and Cixi named the toddler Puyi as heir. She died the next day. His father became regent.

ps.t: At his enthronement in December 1908 the little boy cried and wriggled. His father, kneeling beside him, tried to comfort him by saying it would soon be over, words courtiers later remembered as a bad omen.
ps.why: Told in Puyi's own autobiography, written about fifty years later from what he was told.

ps: He was taken from his mother and raised by eunuchs and wet nurses in the palace. Everyone, including his own family, had to kneel before him. He later wrote that he grew up spoiled, lonely and often cruel to his servants.
October 1911: an army uprising in Wuchang spread across south China. Provinces declared independence and revolutionaries proclaimed a republic, with Sun Yat-sen as its first provisional president.

12 February 1912: the Empress Dowager Longyu signed the abdication on the six-year-old's behalf. Under an agreement with the new Republic he kept his title, a large yearly allowance and the inner half of the Forbidden City.
July 1917: the general Zhang Xun marched into Beijing and put Puyi back on the throne. The restoration lasted twelve days before other warlords' troops ended it.

1919 to 1924: a Scottish tutor, Reginald Johnston, taught him English and about the outside world. Puyi cut off his queue, wore glasses and rode a bicycle in the palace. In 1922 he married Wanrong as empress and Wenxiu as secondary consort.
November 1924: the warlord Feng Yuxiang seized Beijing and expelled him from the Forbidden City. He fled to the Japanese legation and then lived in the Japanese concession in Tianjin.

1931 to 1934: after Japan seized Manchuria, Japanese officers took him there secretly. In 1932 he became Chief Executive of the new state of Manchukuo, and in 1934 its emperor, with the reign name Kangde.
August 1945: as the Soviet army invaded Manchuria and Japan surrendered, he tried to fly to Japan but was captured by Soviet troops at Shenyang airport and held in Siberia.

ps.t: 1946: he testified at the Tokyo war crimes tribunal, describing himself as a helpless prisoner of the Japanese. He later admitted he had hidden his own part in events to protect himself.
ps.why: The testimony is in the tribunal record; the admission is in his autobiography.

ps: 1950 to 1959: the Soviet Union handed him to the People's Republic of China. He spent nine years in the Fushun War Criminals Management Centre, doing labour and 're-education' and writing confessions.

1959 onward: he was pardoned in December 1959. He worked at the Beijing Botanical Garden and then in the archives of a government advisory body, married a nurse, Li Shuxian, in 1962, and died of cancer on 17 October 1967.
His autobiography, published in China in 1964 and in English as From Emperor to Citizen, describes his life from the throne to the prison and his conversion to a new life under communism.
It is a vivid and often self-critical account of court life: the endless rituals, the eunuchs' thefts, the boredom and fears of a boy who was worshipped but not free.
It was written with a ghost-writer, Li Wenda, and checked by officials. It is a key source but also a piece of political rehabilitation, so historians read it with care.
Empress Dowager Cixi (1835 to 1908), who chose him as emperor the day before she died.
Zaifeng, Prince Chun (1883 to 1951), his father and regent from 1908 to 1911.
Reginald Johnston (1874 to 1938), his Scottish tutor, who later wrote Twilight in the Forbidden City.
Wanrong (1906 to 1946), his empress. Isolated and unhappy, she became addicted to opium and died in Communist custody in 1946.
Pujie (1907 to 1994), his younger brother, who married a Japanese noblewoman, Hiro Saga, in a match arranged by the Japanese army.
Sun Yat-sen (1866 to 1925), the revolutionary leader whose movement ended his reign.
The Qianlong Emperor (ruled 1735 to 1796), his great-great-great-grandfather, one of the most powerful Qing rulers, whose palace treasures still surrounded the boy emperor.
The Qing dynasty was weakened by foreign wars, the Taiping rebellion and the Boxer crisis. When Puyi was born, reformers and revolutionaries were already planning its end.
After 1912 China broke into regions ruled by warlords. The Nationalists and Communists fought for control while Japan expanded on the mainland.

Manchukuo was run by the Japanese Kwantung Army, with Japanese officials in key posts. Under its rule people suffered forced labour, the opium trade and brutal repression. Near Harbin the Japanese Unit 731 carried out deadly human experiments. Puyi signed laws and appeared at ceremonies but had little control over any of this.
His life became a symbol of the end of 2,000 years of imperial rule in China, and of the new state's claim that even an emperor could be remade into a citizen.
Bernardo Bertolucci's film The Last Emperor (1987), the first Western feature film allowed to shoot inside the Forbidden City, won nine Academy Awards.
In 1995 his ashes were moved to a cemetery near the Western Qing Tombs, close to his ancestors.

myths.c: The film The Last Emperor shows his life as it was.
myths.t: The main events are real, but the film compresses time and dramatises or invents scenes and relationships. It follows his own autobiography closely, which has its own slant.

myths.c: He was only an innocent puppet.
myths.t: He had very little real power in Manchukuo. But he went there willingly, hoping to restore his dynasty, and he signed what the Japanese put before him. He was both a puppet and a collaborator.

myths.c: He wrote his autobiography on his own.
myths.t: It was prepared with a ghost-writer and edited under official supervision, as part of his public re-education.
He worked at the Beijing Botanical Garden after his release, but from 1964 his job was as a researcher in the archives of a national advisory body.
